sections.title: What is Simulation?
sections.content:
Simulation problems ask you to implement exactly what the problem describes — step by step, no clever algorithm required. The challenge is correctness under edge cases, not finding a smarter approach.

Simulation appears constantly in competitive programming and in interviews as 'design' or 'implement this game' problems. Game of Life, robot navigation, spiral traversal, and snake game are all simulation — the algorithm is the problem statement.

Critical judgment call: **when is direct simulation within the time limit?** n ≤ 10³ and steps ≤ 10³ → O(10⁶) — fine. Steps can be 10⁹ → need a shortcut. Most common shortcut: **cycle detection**. Finite state must eventually cycle. Find cycle length L, skip full cycles, simulate only the remainder.

Recognizing when to simulate vs when to optimize is a meta-skill that comes from practice.

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: Simulate when the problem explicitly describes a process and constraints are small enough. Estimate O(n × steps) and compare to ~10^8 operations. Also simulate when the state space is finite and you can detect cycles to skip ahead.

sections.title: Cycle Detection, Direction Arrays, and Event-Driven Simulation
sections.content:
## When to Simulate Directly

n ≤ 10³ and steps ≤ 10³: O(10⁶) — simulate freely. n ≤ 10⁴ and steps ≤ 10⁴: O(10⁸) — borderline. Steps ≤ 10⁹: must find a shortcut.

## Cycle Detection

1. Store visited states: `{ serializedState → stepIndex }`.
2. At each step, serialize current state.
3. If seen before: `cycleLen = currentStep - seen[state]`.
4. Remaining steps after cycle start: `(totalSteps - cycleStart) % cycleLen`.
5. Simulate that many more steps.

## Direction Arrays

```
dirs = [[0,1],[1,0],[0,-1],[-1,0]]  // right, down, left, up
dirIdx = 0
```
Turn right: `(dirIdx+1)%4`. Turn left: `(dirIdx+3)%4`. Move: `[r+dirs[dirIdx][0], c+dirs[dirIdx][1]]`.

## State Mutation Hazard (Game of Life)

When all cells update simultaneously, reading an already-updated neighbor corrupts results. Use a copy of the current state for reads, write to a separate buffer. Or encode both states in the cell value.

## Event-Driven Simulation

Only process steps where something changes. Reduces O(T) to O(E) where T is total time span and E is number of events.

sections.title: Recognizing When Plain Simulation Won't Finish
sections.content:
The single most important judgment call in a simulation problem is checking the constraints BEFORE writing any code: if the number of steps is small (roughly <= 10^6 total operations), simulate directly - it's the simplest correct approach and no cleverness is needed. If the step count is large (10^9 or more) but the STATE SPACE is small and finite (a bounded grid position + direction, a small set of possible configurations), that's the signal for the cycle-detection approach already covered - the process must eventually repeat a state, so simulate only until a repeat is found, then jump forward mathematically using the cycle length instead of simulating every remaining step.

If neither applies - the step count is huge AND the state space is also effectively unbounded (e.g. simulating a physical quantity that grows without a repeating pattern) - that's usually a signal the problem isn't meant to be brute-force simulated at all, and there's a closed-form formula, a mathematical shortcut (matrix exponentiation for linear recurrences, for instance), or a different technique entirely being tested instead of simulation. Recognizing which of these three buckets a problem falls into, from the constraints alone, before writing any simulation code, is the actual skill this topic tests - the simulation code itself is usually the easy part once the right bucket is identified.

sections.title: Core Template
sections.explanation: Direction array template for clean grid movement with turn support. Cycle detection template finds cycle start and length then simulates only the necessary remainder.

items.name: Parallel State Update (Game of Life)
items.description: All cells update simultaneously based on current state. Must read from old state and write to new — never mix. Use a copy or encode old and new state in the same cell value using different bits.

items.name: Robot Bounded in Circle
items.description: After one full instruction cycle, the robot is bounded if it is back at the origin OR not facing north. Simulate one cycle and check position and final direction.

items.name: Spiral Matrix Traversal
items.description: Maintain four boundaries (top, bottom, left, right). Peel one layer per cycle: top row, right column, bottom row, left column. Shrink boundaries after each side. Stop when top > bottom or left > right.

sections.title: Complexity
sections.time: O(n × steps) direct; O(stateSpace + cycleLength) with cycle detection
sections.space: O(stateSpace) for cycle detection map; O(1) extra for direct grid simulation
sections.explanation: Direct simulation: O(steps) steps with O(n) work per step if iterating over n-element state. With cycle detection: store at most one entry per unique state, find cycle in O(stateSpace) steps, then simulate at most cycleLength additional steps. Grid traversal visits every cell once: O(rows × cols).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Mutating state while reading it in parallel-update problems (Game of Life): writing grid[r][c]=newVal before all neighbors are processed reads the new value for cells that should use the old. Always read from a copy.
Turn-left using dirIdx-1: gives -1 when dirIdx is 0, which wraps to wrong index. Use (dirIdx+3)%4.
Boundary check after moving instead of before: compute new position, validate it, then update. Stepping to an invalid position first causes index-out-of-bounds errors.

Cycle detection serialization: JSON.stringify works but is slow for large states. Custom hash improves performance. Ensure serialization is injective — different states must produce different strings.
Not applying cycle detection when step count is large: if k=10^9 but state space is 10^4, simulating all k steps causes TLE when the cycle is guaranteed to appear before 10^4 steps.

items.title: Game of Life
items.why: Parallel state update — tests simultaneous-update pattern where old state must be preserved for all cells before any new state is written.

items.title: Robot Bounded in Circle
items.why: Direction array + cycle reasoning — simulate one cycle and check position and direction to determine boundedness.

items.title: Spiral Matrix
items.why: Boundary-peeling simulation — tests four shrinking boundaries and edge cases where only one row or column remains.

items.title: Walking Robot Simulation
items.why: Direction array + obstacle hash set — combines grid movement with O(1) collision detection using a set of obstacle coordinates.
